name: Archimedes' crown and the balance that would actually have worked
scope: Buoyancy as a lie detector -- and the physics behind the story the history bank already tells. T1: a steel nail dropped in a bucket goes straight down, yet a steel ship floats; the rule Archimedes set down in On Floating Bodies is that a fluid pushes up on anything dunked in it with a force equal to the weight of the fluid shoved out of the way (teach 'displace' here). T2: why silver betrays a goldsmith -- gold runs about 19.3 grams per cubic centimetre and silver only about 10.5, so a crown of the SAME weight with silver blended in must be BULKIER; the fraud can never show up as extra weight on a dry scale, only as extra size. T3: in 1586 a 22-year-old Galileo published La Bilancetta ('The Little Balance') arguing that the overflow method Vitruvius describes could never have worked, because the difference in spilled water would be far too small for any ancient instrument to read -- and proposed instead a hydrostatic balance: hang the crown from a scale arm, weigh it in air, then lower it into water and read how much apparent weight it LOSES. T4: the mechanism nobody mentions -- water does not 'know' what it displaced; the bottom face of a submerged object sits deeper, where water squeezes harder, than the top face, and that up-push minus down-push comes out exactly equal to the displaced weight. T5: the rule's own breaking point -- a smooth flat block sealed against the bottom of a tank, with no water able to reach underneath it, feels no upward push at all and stays put; 'weight of displaced fluid' is a shorthand for pressure acting on every face, not a law about displacement. Further rungs: a floating thing sinks only until it has shoved aside its OWN weight, which is why loading cargo makes a hull ride lower until it has displaced exactly the extra weight; buoyancy is not a water law -- a helium balloon rises for the same reason a cork does, because the AIR it shoves aside outweighs it; a hydrometer rides high in dense liquid and low in thin, and an egg that sinks in tap water floats once enough salt is stirred in; you weigh less standing in a swimming pool because the scale reads your weight minus the weight of a you-shaped piece of water.
source: Grokipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' (accessed 2026-08-11) -- F_B = rho_f*V*g; principle stated in On Floating Bodies, 3rd c. BCE; the Eureka bath tale flagged as likely apocryphal with Vitruvius's De Architectura (1st c. BCE, ~200 years later) as the sole surviving source; buoyancy arising from pressure difference in a static fluid. Wikipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' -- the limitation that the principle fails when an object's face touches the vessel bottom or wall so fluid cannot reach it; the alternative balance-in-air-then-submerged method. Chris Rorres, 'The Golden Crown: La Bilancetta' (math.nyu.edu/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html) and Museo Galileo, 'Weighing instruments' -- Galileo's 1586 La Bilancetta, written at 22, arguing the Vitruvian overflow test demanded precision unavailable in antiquity, and describing his hydrostatic balance based on Archimedes' laws of the lever and of buoyancy.
framing_note: MECHANISM ladder on a discovery spine. THE governing rail: the HISTORY bank already owns the crown STORY -- science owns only the physics. The bathtub/Eureka tale may appear in CONTEXT as a legend and must never be a stem hook or an answer; note honestly that Archimedes' surviving On Floating Bodies contains the principle and says nothing whatever about a crown. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- 'the famous method probably would not have worked, and here is the one that would' is the test-it-yourself soul compressed into one rung, and a kid can run Galileo's version with a kitchen scale and a mug. Distractor mine: horror vacui; 'floating is about shape, not density'; 'the water pushes back on what does not belong'; plus the real rival ancient assay methods a goldsmith actually faced -- the touchstone streak test, comparing hardness, ringing the metal for tone. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'because silver is less dense' before asking what gives the fraud away. Teach 'displace' and 'density' before any rung leans on them.
history_overlap: HEAVY. HISTORY bank owns the Archimedes crown ladder outright: a T1 rung whose answer is 'Eureka! -- I have found it!', a T2 rung 'King Hiero... what did he measure?' answered 'how much water each one pushed out of a tub', plus the Archimedes screw, the ship-pulling with compound pulleys, the Claw, the heat-ray legend, the sphere-in-cylinder tomb and Cicero's search, and a context line already crediting Vitruvius writing ~200 years later. None of those facts may be re-asked here. GEOGRAPHY owns the iceberg's 'about 90% underwater' fact (T1) -- do not re-ask it. ANIMAL owns nautilus and cuttlebone buoyancy, including a rung whose answer is already 'a submarine' -- keep submarines, swim bladders and all creatures out of this ladder.

name: Torricelli's ocean of air
scope: The instrument that proved we live at the bottom of a sea that weighs on us. T1: in Florence in 1643 Evangelista Torricelli -- Galileo's assistant during the old man's last blind months -- filled a metre-long glass tube with mercury, upended it into a dish, and the mercury slid down and then STOPPED, standing at about 76 cm with an empty gap above it that nothing had ever filled; the answer is the first sustained man-made vacuum, still called the Torricellian vacuum. T2: what holds the column up. In a letter of 11 June 1644 to Michelangelo Ricci he wrote 'Noi viviamo sommersi nel fondo d'un pelago d'aria' -- we live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air -- and said it is the weight of that air, pressing down on the open dish, that holds the mercury aloft. T3: why mercury. Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, so the air can support only 76 cm of it; the same air supports about 10.3 metres of water, and a water barometer needs a tube taller than a three-storey house -- Gasparo Berti had in fact built one in Rome around 1640, a lead pipe running up the outside of his house. T4: the reigning theory this overturned -- Aristotle's horror vacui, that nature abhors a void and the liquid is held up by nature's refusal to permit emptiness. Torricelli's account made a prediction the abhorrence account could not: the height must depend on how much air happens to be stacked above you. T5: the instrument nobody ordered -- at one fixed place the column drifts up and down from day to day, which means the ocean of air itself is not steady; that wobble is the entire content of a modern barometer, and a falling column still means weather coming. Further rungs: about ten tonnes of air rests on an adult body and you never feel it because the same pressure pushes out from inside; Torricelli's law -- water squirting from a hole in a tank leaves at the speed it would have reached falling from the water's surface, testable with a punched milk jug; Torricelli died of a fever at 39 in October 1647, so the mountain test that vindicated him was run the year after his death.
source: Grokipedia, 'Evangelista Torricelli' (accessed 2026-08-11) -- first mercury barometer 1643; assistant to the blind Galileo at Arcetri from Oct 1641 to Galileo's death 8 Jan 1642; succeeded him as court mathematician to Grand Duke Ferdinando II; correspondence with Michelangelo Ricci and Marin Mersenne; died 25 Oct 1647 of a fever, likely typhoid, aged 39. Wikipedia, 'Evangelista Torricelli' -- the exact Italian wording of the quote and its provenance in the 11 June 1644 letter to Ricci; the ~76 cm column and the Torricellian vacuum; the column's fluctuation with atmospheric pressure underpinning weather forecasting. Wikipedia, 'Barometer' -- Gasparo Berti's water barometer built between roughly 1640 and 1643 with Magiotti, Kircher and Zucchi present; mercury about 14 times denser than water, allowing a manageable ~80 cm tube instead of ~10.5 m; 1644 the more probable date Torricelli first reported results.
framing_note: The strand's keystone DISCOVERY ladder; every later ladder in this sub-strand leans on it. Accuracy rail: the quote IS documented, but quote only the short attested form and always tie it to the 11 June 1644 letter to Michelangelo Ricci -- the longer English versions circulating online ('...which by unquestioned experiments is known to have weight') are a translator's continuation, so either cite the full letter or stay with the short form. Second rail: 1643 is the conventional date but the first reported results are 1644; since bare dates are banned as answers this only matters for context wording. Dinner-test payoff: T2, the sentence itself -- a kid repeating 'we live at the bottom of an ocean of air' at the table is the whole sub-strand in one line. Distractor mine: horror vacui, Linus's funiculus (an invisible thread of stretched matter), 'the glass holds it', 'mercury is magnetic', the ether -- respectable-but-wrong seventeenth-century live options. Lane inside this strand: the 10.3 m water ceiling and the suction-pump story belong to the STRAW ladder; this ladder keeps mercury, the vacuum, the ocean-of-air sentence and the weather.

name: Pascal and the weight of fluids: the claim tested on a mountain
scope: A prediction, a mountain, and the first properly controlled experiment most people have never heard of. T1: Blaise Pascal was too ill to climb anything, so on 19 September 1648 his brother-in-law Florin Perier carried a mercury barometer up the Puy de Dome in the Auvergne on Pascal's instructions -- the answer is the relative who did the legwork for another man's prediction. T2: the prediction and the result. If the mercury is held up by the weight of the air stacked above it, then climbing leaves less air above you and the column must FALL. In the monastery garden at the foot it stood at 26 inches 3-and-a-half lines; at the summit, roughly a kilometre higher, 23 inches 2 lines -- a drop of about three French inches, some 8 cm. T3: THE CONTROL -- the rung that makes 1648 look modern. Perier left a second barometer at the base and had Father Chastin of the Minim brothers watch it all day, so that if the summit reading fell they could prove the air had not simply shifted everywhere at once. T4: the scaling check -- Pascal repeated the test on the tower of Saint-Jacques in Paris, only about 50 m tall, and found a drop of about two lines. The effect tracking height is what turned one mountain reading into a rule, and what makes a barometer an ALTIMETER: the instrument in every aircraft that reads altitude by reading pressure. T5: Pascal's other half -- pressure applied anywhere in a trapped liquid is passed on undiminished to every part of it, which is why a thin arm on a car jack lifts two tonnes: a small piston travels a long way so a large piston can travel a short way with an enormous force, trading distance for force and creating no energy at all. Further rungs: the hydrostatic paradox -- pressure at the bottom depends only on DEPTH, so a thin pipe of water a metre tall presses exactly as hard as a metre-deep lake; Pascal's barrel, the tale of a sealed cask burst by a few cups poured down a long thin pipe, told AS a story since it appears nowhere in Pascal's surviving works and looks like a nineteenth-century French invention (creve-tonneau); the priority quarrel in which Descartes claimed he had suggested the mountain test and Pascal's circle denied it; why your ears pop in a lift.
source: Grokipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' (accessed 2026-08-11) -- learned of Torricelli through Mersenne and replicated it in 1646; instructed Florin Perier to test the prediction on the Puy de Dome; 19 September 1648, two tubes filled at a monastery at the base, reduced height at the summit with no change on tilting or shaking; Perier's report letter of 22 September 1648; Denis Papin's and other critiques; the altitude test as a falsifiable prediction. Wikipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' -- base reading 26 inches 3-and-a-half lines and summit reading 23 inches 2 lines; Father Chastin of the Minim Brothers stationed at the monastery base to watch for changes through the day; the Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie tower repeat (~50 m) showing a two-line drop; Experiences nouvelles touchant le vide (1647) and Recit de la grande experience de l'equilibre des liqueurs (1648); the route to the hydraulic press. Wikipedia, 'Pascal's barrel' -- usually dated 1646, mentioned nowhere in Pascal's preserved works, likely attributed by nineteenth-century French authors, illustrating the hydrostatic paradox.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder whose real subject is what a good test looks like -- falsification as WORKING PRACTICE, which is science's lane, not philosophy's seminar. Accuracy rail: use Perier's actual figures (26 in 3.5 lines at the base, 23 in 2 lines at the summit, a drop of about three French inches / ~8 cm). Several secondary sources round this to 'about 27 inches down to 23' -- that is wrong; do not seed it. Second rail: Pascal's barrel must be told AS a probably-apocryphal story, never as something Pascal did. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- the control barometer with a monk watching it all day is the single most 'this is how you build an honest test' fact in the sub-strand, and it lands with a ten-year-old. Distractor mine: horror vacui; 'the mountain air is thinner because it is colder'; Descartes' subtle matter filling the plenum; the ether; plus Descartes himself as a real attribution distractor for who proposed the test. Anti-restatement: describe the two readings and the man watching the base instrument, and let the PURPOSE of the second barometer be recalled knowledge, not deduced from a stem clause.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank has a T3 Pascal rung that uses 'carried a barometer up the Puy-de-Dome to weigh the air' purely as scene-setting, with the answer being the Pensees line about the eternal silence of infinite spaces -- no fact clash, but this ladder must stay entirely off Pascal's wager, the Pensees and his religious writing, which are philosophy's. The OLD science bank being replaced carries a definition-shell T2 ('Pascal showed liquids in a closed system carry pressure... pressure applied anywhere is transmitted unchanged') -- this ladder supersedes it and must not reproduce its bare-definition form.

name: What two teams of horses could not pull apart
scope: The demonstration that turned an invisible force into a public argument. T1: two copper half-spheres about 50 cm across, greased at the rim and simply pressed together -- no bolt, no catch, no glue. Once Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of them, teams of horses hauling in opposite directions could not part them; when he opened a small valve they fell into his hands. The answer: nothing was holding them together at all, the outside air was pressing them shut. T2: who did it -- Guericke was burgomaster of Magdeburg, a city where roughly four-fifths of more than 25,000 people had been killed in the 1631 sack; he rebuilt it for thirty years and invented the first working air pump around 1650 in his spare hours. T3: the honest deflation -- the two opposing teams were showmanship. One team pulling against a stone wall would have proved exactly the same thing, because the wall supplies the equal and opposite pull for nothing. T4: the size of it -- with a good vacuum inside, ordinary air presses a 50 cm sphere shut with something like 20 kilonewtons, about the weight of a small car; and the number comes from the pressure times the area of the flat CIRCLE where the two halves meet, not the whole curved surface. Further rungs: Guericke's quieter demonstrations -- a piston that a crowd of strong men could not hold back once the air was drawn out, a bell rung inside an evacuated jar that could not be heard, a candle that went out; why the shape had to be a sphere, since anything with a flat face would have crumpled; and the provenance of the famous picture -- the engraving everyone reproduces comes from Gaspar Schott's Mechanica Hydraulico-Pneumatica of 1657, printed before Guericke's own Experimenta Nova of 1672.
source: Wikipedia, 'Magdeburg hemispheres' -- Guericke as mayor of Magdeburg and inventor of the first vacuum pump (piston and cylinder with one-way flap valves); hemispheres ~50 cm / 20 inches across; ~20 kN of holding force, 'equivalent to lifting a car'; 8 May 1654 Regensburg display before Emperor Ferdinand III and the Imperial Diet with thirty horses in two teams of fifteen; 1656 Magdeburg with sixteen horses in two teams of eight; 1663 Berlin with twenty-four horses before the Great Elector; the explicit note that a stationary anchor would produce an identical result and the horse teams were theatrical; sound could not cross the evacuated sphere. Wikipedia, 'Otto von Guericke' -- Burgomeister of Magdeburg 1646-1678; the May 1631 sack in which around eighty percent of 25,000-plus inhabitants died; vacuum pump around 1650; the piston-against-many-men, extinguished-flame and air-has-weight demonstrations; first publication in Gaspar Schott's Mechanica Hydraulico-pneumatica (1657), then Technica Curiosa (1664), then Experimenta Nova (1672).
framing_note: DEMONSTRATION ladder -- the wonder is that a public spectacle can be a rigorous argument. THE accuracy rail: sources genuinely disagree on how many horses (thirty at Regensburg 1654, sixteen at Magdeburg 1656, twenty-four at Berlin 1663), so a horse count must NEVER be an answer or a distractor set; the answer is always the physics or the act. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- the horses were theatre and one team plus a wall would have done it. That rung teaches Newton's third law without naming it and it is exactly the bank's skepticism-of-the-impressive reflex. Distractor mine: horror vacui / 'nature abhors a vacuum'; suction imagined as a pulling force; magnetism; a hidden latch or glue; Linus's funiculus. Teach 'vacuum' and 'air pressure' before testing them. Lane: HISTORY owns the Thirty Years' War as narrative -- the 1631 sack may occupy one clause of scene-setting for who Guericke was and must never be an answer.
history_overlap: None found: a keyword sweep of the shipped history, geography, animal, philosophy, cooking and trivia banks returned no Guericke and no Magdeburg-hemispheres question (history's only 'Magdeburg' hit is Krakow's market square laid out under Magdeburg law, unrelated). Border to respect: HISTORY owns the Thirty Years' War and the 1631 sack of Magdeburg as war history.

name: Boyle, Hooke and the spring of the air
scope: A famous law whose namesake credited someone else, and the fight over whether emptiness can exist. T1: air pushes back. Trap air in a syringe with your finger over the nozzle and press -- it springs back; Robert Boyle called that push-back 'the spring of the air'. T2: the measurement, in the 1660s, with a young Robert Hooke building the apparatus: air sealed into the short closed arm of a J-shaped glass tube, mercury poured down the long open arm; double the squeeze and the trapped air shrank to half its length. T3: the honest-credit rung -- Boyle did not claim the rule as his own idea. He credited 'Mr Towneley's hypothesis', after Richard Towneley and Henry Power, who had put the inverse relation to him; and in France the same rule is taught as Mariotte's law after Edme Mariotte found it independently and added the condition Boyle had left unsaid, that the temperature must be held steady. T4: the fight -- Thomas Hobbes attacked the whole air-pump enterprise in Dialogus physicus (1661), arguing a true void was impossible and the pump must simply be leaking; the Jesuit Franciscus Linus insisted an invisible 'funiculus', a thread of stretched matter, was doing the holding. Boyle answered with more experiments rather than more argument. T5: what the spring actually is -- air is mostly empty space with molecules flying about, and pressure is the drumming of those molecules on the walls; halve the space and every wall gets hit twice as often. Daniel Bernoulli wrote this out in Hydrodynamica in 1738 and used it to explain Boyle's law, a century before anyone could see a molecule. Further rungs: Boyle put birds, mice, eels, snails and flies into the evacuated receiver to show that living things depend on air, and a hundred years later travelling lecturers made 'the animal in the air pump' the paid showpiece of an evening's entertainment -- which is the scene Joseph Wright of Derby painted in 1768, with the lecturer staring straight out of the canvas at the viewer; a marshmallow or a half-inflated balloon swelling under a bell jar; and why a sealed bag of crisps puffs up on an aircraft.
source: Wikipedia, 'Boyle's law' -- published 1662; assistant Robert Hooke constructed the apparatus; the closed J-shaped tube with mercury compressing trapped air; Richard Towneley and Henry Power first noting the relationship, acknowledged by Boyle as 'Towneley's hypothesis'; Edme Mariotte's independent discovery and his addition of the temperature condition, hence the dual naming; described as the first physical law expressed as an equation relating two variables. Wikipedia, 'An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump' -- Wright of Derby, 1768; the scene depicts an itinerant lecturer's paid public performance rather than formal research; Boyle's 1660s trials in the 1660s with birds, mice, eels, snails and flies to study living creatures' reliance on air. Wikipedia, 'Daniel Bernoulli' and 'Bernoulli's principle' -- Hydrodynamica (1738) laid the basis of the kinetic theory of gases and applied it to explain Boyle's law.
framing_note: CONCEPT ladder carrying native T4/T5 ceiling for the sub-strand's analytic backbone. THE accuracy rail: Boyle's law was not solely Boyle's discovery and the bank must say so -- he publicly credited Towneley and Power, and Mariotte found it independently and supplied the constant-temperature condition. The honest-credit rung is the point of the ladder, not a footnote, and Hooke must be named as the man who built the pump rather than filed away as 'an assistant'. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- a law named for a man who told everyone it was someone else's idea. Distractor mine: the funiculus, horror vacui, caloric, phlogiston, the ether, and the real people -- Towneley, Power, Mariotte, Hooke, Hobbes -- as attribution distractors, every one of them a live historical possibility. Teach 'pressure' and 'vacuum' before any rung leans on them; NEVER test PV = k as a symbol, and never ask what a letter stands for -- that is banned rote.

name: How a wing really lifts, and why the textbook story is wrong
scope: The corrected misconception at the centre of this whole sub-strand. T2: the story almost every schoolbook and museum placard tells -- the air splitting at the front of a wing has farther to go over the humped top than under the flat bottom, so it must hurry to rejoin its partner at the trailing edge; faster air has lower pressure, so the wing is sucked upward. T3: how we know it is wrong. Holger Babinsky at Cambridge filmed pulses of smoke flowing over an aerofoil and published the frames in Physics Education in 2003: the smoke over the TOP reaches the trailing edge well before the smoke underneath does. The top air is not merely as fast as the story requires -- it arrives early and has already left the wing behind by the time the bottom air catches up. There was never any reason the two parcels had to meet again. T4: what actually happens -- a wing throws a great deal of air DOWNWARD, and by Newton's third law that air pushes the wing up; you can see the downwash in a helicopter's rotor wash and in flattened wheat under a low-flying aircraft. T5: the two accounts are one account. The pressure field and the turned flow cause each other; the requirement that flow leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly (the Kutta condition) fixes how much circulation runs around the wing, and that circulation IS the lift. Further rungs: the killer test -- an aeroplane can fly upside down, because a cambered wing inverted still lifts once it is tilted enough, and a flat balsa glider wing with no hump at all flies perfectly well, so shape is not what makes lift; where Bernoulli's principle is genuinely right and useful (an atomiser, a carburettor, a Venturi throat) so the kid learns the equation is sound and only the equal-transit reasoning is not; the paper-strip demonstration told honestly, since the air leaving your mouth is at room pressure and what does the work is the curving of the streamlines; the stall, where past roughly fifteen degrees the flow separates and lift collapses because the wing has stopped turning air; and Henri Pitot, who in 1732 pushed a bent tube into the Seine to measure how fast a river runs, whose descendant on a wing's leading edge tells a pilot the airspeed -- and which, iced over or plugged by a mud-dauber wasp's nest, has killed (Air France 447, Birgenair 301).
source: Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)' -- 'The assumption of equal transit time is wrong when applied to a body generating lift. There is no physical principle that requires equal transit time'; the air over the top of a lifting aerofoil 'moves much faster than equal transit time predicts'; the flow-turning / Newton's-third-law description characterised as correct but incomplete; the mutual interaction of pressure differences and flow velocity; the Kutta condition and the Kutta-Joukowski theorem; the explanation of inverted flight via angle of attack on a cambered aerofoil. Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle' -- the misunderstandings section, including that the air leaving a demonstrator's mouth is at the same pressure as the room so the blown-paper demonstration is not a Bernoulli demonstration, the ball-in-a-jet being asymmetric flow rather than low pressure, and 'the air traverses the top surface... in a shorter time than it traverses the bottom surface'. Holger Babinsky, 'How do wings work?', Physics Education 38(6), 2003 -- the smoke-pulse films showing unequal transit and the streamline-curvature / pressure-gradient analysis. Wikipedia, 'Pitot tube' -- Pitot's 1732 publication, stagnation versus static pressure, Darcy's 1858 modern form, airspeed use, and the Air France 447 icing and Birgenair 301 blocked-tube accidents.
framing_note: The sub-strand's FLAGSHIP corrected-misconception ladder and, arguably, the reason the strand exists: an explanation printed in every schoolbook and endorsed by museums is wrong, and a man with a smoke tunnel and a camera showed it. TWO accuracy rails, both essential. First: do NOT overcorrect into 'Bernoulli is wrong' -- Bernoulli's principle is correct physics; what is wrong is the equal-transit-time reasoning bolted onto it, and a rung must make that distinction explicitly. Second: do not present 'wings push air down' as the whole truth either -- the sources call the Newtonian account correct but incomplete, so the honest T5 says the pressure field and the turned flow cause each other. Dinner-test payoff: the Babinsky smoke-pulse rung, where the top air arrives FIRST, backed by the upside-down-flight rung a kid can half-check by throwing a flat balsa glider. Anti-restatement is unusually delicate here: the stem sets up the classroom story and the smoke film, and must never contain the phrase that gives away 'they do not have to meet again'. Distractor mine is exceptionally rich -- the equal-transit story itself, 'suction from a vacuum above the wing', 'the engines push it up', the Coanda effect misapplied, and the genuinely respectable partial answers (circulation alone, Newton alone) as adjacent-but-incomplete options. Lane: ANIMAL owns bird and bat flight adaptation, including its own wind-tunnel rungs on the peregrine and the humpback-flipper tubercle wing -- no creature is the subject of any rung here.
history_overlap: The OLD science bank being replaced contains exactly the errors this ladder corrects -- a T2 'Daniel Bernoulli... described why airplanes can fly / faster-moving fluid exerts lower pressure' and a T2 two-paper-strips question explained by naive Bernoulli. Both are superseded, and the build should treat them as the misconception to be dismantled, not as facts to preserve. ANIMAL bank owns a T4 humpback-tubercle wind-tunnel rung and a T4 peregrine wind-tunnel rung -- no animal aerodynamics here.

name: Two bicycle mechanics build their own wind tunnel
scope: Not the flight -- the INSTRUMENT, and what it means to distrust the published numbers. T2: the machine itself, built in the back of a bicycle shop in Dayton in the autumn of 1901: a wooden box about six feet long with a sixteen-inch-square throat, a fan driven off the shop's engine giving a steady wind of roughly twenty-five miles an hour, and a glass window in the lid to watch through. T3: the cleverest part, and the answer that carries the ladder -- the balances inside, cut and bent from old hacksaw blades and bicycle spoke wire. They were built to read the RATIO of lift to drag directly, so the result did not depend on knowing the air's density or the disputed Smeaton constant at all: an instrument deliberately designed so that the numbers nobody could trust cancel themselves out. T4: what the data changed in the wing -- the deep one-in-twelve arch everyone had copied from bird wings was wrong, and a shallow camber near one in twenty lifted better for the drag it cost; and long narrow wings with a high aspect ratio, around six or seven, badly beat short stubby ones. T5: the epistemic rung -- the tables they threw away were not cranks' work. They were the published measurements of Otto Lilienthal, the most experienced glider pilot alive, reprinted under the Smithsonian's name. Two men with no degree, no funding and no laboratory re-measured the foundation of a field in about two months, and were right. Further rungs: the scaling bet that makes wind tunnels possible at all -- a model wing a few inches across in a fast wind behaves like a large wing in a slower one, which is why you can test an aeroplane on a workbench; and the descendants, from full-size automotive tunnels to NASA's, all running the same idea.
source: Grokipedia, 'Wright brothers' (accessed 2026-08-11) -- 1901 wind tunnel in the Dayton bicycle shop, a wooden box roughly 6 feet long with a 16-inch square test section, gas-engine-driven fan producing about 25 mph; between 100 and 200 small-scale wing models tested with about 30 selected for detailed evaluation on custom balances measuring lift and drag at various angles of attack; the Lilienthal tables published by the Smithsonian overestimating lift by a factor of three; optimum camber around 1 in 20 rather than the deeper 1 in 12; aspect ratios around 6 to 7 giving superior performance by reducing induced drag; the 1902 glider's 700-1,000 glides and best of 622.5 feet. Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers' -- the 1901 glider producing about one third of calculated lift; Wilbur's dejected remark that man would not fly in a thousand years; the accepted Smeaton coefficient of 0.0054 versus the roughly 0.0033 Wilbur derived; balances made from bicycle spokes and scrap metal / hacksaw blades; about 200 wings tested with 38 analysed in detail.
framing_note: The strand's TEST-IT-YOURSELF flagship, but the lane is narrow because the history bank already owns the Wright story in depth, INCLUDING two wind-tunnel rungs. BANNED here, all owned by history: the 17 December 1903 flight and its 12 seconds / 120 feet / 852 feet in 59 seconds; wing-warping; Charlie Taylor and the engine; the propeller-as-a-rotating-wing insight; the coin toss; the 1878 toy helicopter; the gust that wrecked the Flyer; Armstrong carrying Flyer fabric to the Moon; and above all the two facts history already keys to the tunnel -- 'their wing made about a third of the lift Lilienthal's tables predicted' and 'the Smeaton coefficient was off by nearly a factor of two'. Build instead on the box and fan, the hacksaw-blade balances, the ratio trick, camber and aspect ratio, model scaling and the epistemics. Dinner-test payoff: the balances -- an instrument designed so the untrusted constant cancels. Accuracy rail: model counts genuinely differ between good sources (100-200 screened, roughly 30 to 38 measured in detail), so never make a count the answer or a numeric distractor set. Distractor mine: real rival authorities and their real wrong numbers -- Lilienthal's tables, Samuel Langley's stability-first school and his funded failure, Octave Chanute, the Smeaton constant -- plus 'they copied birds' and 'they guessed'.
history_overlap: HEAVY -- the largest overlap in this sub-strand. HISTORY bank owns a full Wright ladder: T1 the 1878 toy helicopter their father brought home; T2 the 12 seconds on 17 December 1903; T2 wing-warping as their great insight; T3 Charlie Taylor building the engine; T3 the coin flip and Wilbur's failed 14 December attempt; T3 the gust that wrecked the Flyer; T4 the four flights and 852 feet in 59 seconds; T4 propellers as rotating wings; T4 'In 1901 the Wright brothers built a wooden wind tunnel... their wing made only about a third of the lift his tables predicted'; T5 'the Smeaton coefficient... off by nearly a factor of two'; plus Armstrong's 1969 Flyer relic. Every one of those is off-limits here. This ladder is confined to the instrument, the measurement method, the aerodynamic findings (camber, aspect ratio, scaling) and the epistemic lesson.

name: A sheep, a duck and a rooster fly first
scope: The first air passengers, and two brothers who were wrong about their own machine. T1: on 19 September 1783, in the forecourt at Versailles, Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette watched the first passengers in the history of flight go up under a Montgolfier balloon -- a sheep called Montauciel ('Climb-to-the-sky'), a duck and a rooster. Eight minutes and about three kilometres later all three came down alive. T2: why those three -- the sheep as a stand-in for a human being, the duck as a comparison animal already known to survive at altitude, and the rooster as a bird that does not fly high. A public spectacle with a comparison group built into it. T3: the brothers were wrong about their own balloon. Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier were paper makers who believed the SMOKE was the buoyant part, burned damp straw and wool to make more of it, and spoke of a special 'Montgolfier gas'. The balloon rose because heating air spreads it thinner, so the colder air outside outweighs it -- density, not smoke. T4: the rival technology, within weeks. Jacques Charles flew hydrogen instead of hot air; his first unmanned hydrogen balloon came down at Gonesse on 27 August 1783 and terrified villagers tore it apart with pitchforks and knives. On 1 December 1783 he flew with Nicolas-Louis Robert from the Tuileries, then went up alone to about three thousand metres, where the pain in his ears was so severe that he never flew again. Further rungs: 4 June 1783 at Annonay, the first public demonstration, roughly two kilometres in ten minutes; 21 November 1783, Pilatre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes making the first free human flight, about twenty-five minutes over Paris; the two rival machines needing opposite controls -- a hot-air balloon carries a burner and a vent, a gas balloon carries ballast to drop and gas to release; and the modern descendant, a weather balloon that swells as it climbs into thinner air until it bursts.
source: Wikipedia, 'Montgolfier brothers' -- Joseph-Michel (1740-1810) and Jacques-Etienne (1745-1799), paper manufacturers of Annonay; 4 June 1783 Annonay demonstration covering 2 km in 10 minutes; 19 September 1783 Aerostat Reveillon at Versailles before Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette carrying the sheep Montauciel, a duck and a rooster, about eight minutes, three kilometres, roughly 500 m altitude, all animals surviving; the brothers' belief that the smoke itself was the buoyant part and their 'Montgolfier gas'; 21 November 1783 first free manned flight by Pilatre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes, about 900 m up over Paris, nine kilometres, twenty-five minutes. Wikipedia, 'Jacques Charles' -- 27 August 1783 unmanned 35-cubic-metre rubberised-silk hydrogen balloon from the Champ de Mars, 45 minutes aloft, landing at Gonesse where terrified peasants destroyed it with pitchforks or knives; 1 December 1783 manned flight with Nicolas-Louis Robert from the Tuileries, 1:45 pm, about 550 m, 2 hours 5 minutes, 36 km to Nesles-la-Vallee; Charles's solo re-ascent to about 3,000 m, the ear pain, and that he never flew again.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder whose payoff is the animal crew at T1 -- the single most repeatable dinner-table fact in this sub-strand, and a ten-year-old can picture it whole. Accuracy rail: the Montgolfiers were WRONG about their own machine, believing the smoke lifted it, and that must be told as a corrected misconception rather than smoothed over; no rung may imply they understood density. Second rail: do NOT seed Benjamin Franklin's 'what use is a newborn baby?' remark -- the attribution is not securely documented, and unsourced quotes are banned. Distractor mine: 'Montgolfier gas', smoke as the lifting agent, phlogiston, 'the fire pushes down against the ground', hydrogen-versus-hot-air confusions, and Jacques Charles as a real rival attribution. Lane: GEOGRAPHY owns hot-air balloons as place-spectacle, so no rung may be about where balloons fly today; and the old science bank's definition-shell T1 ('a hot-air balloon floats up because warm air is less dense') is replaced here by a scene with a named sheep in it.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank owns hot-air balloons as PLACE spectacle -- a T1 on roughly 2,000 balloons over Bagan and a T2 whose answer is 'hot-air balloons' rising over Cappadocia at dawn. Keep every rung on the 1783 discovery and its physics, never on modern ballooning destinations. HISTORY owns Leonardo's aerial-screw and parachute sketches and the entire Wright/Kitty Hawk narrative; this ladder stops in the 1780s and never runs forward to powered flight.

name: Float a steel paperclip, then touch it with soap
scope: The kid-replicable heart of the sub-strand, and a woman who measured a molecule at her kitchen sink. T1: a steel paperclip is nearly eight times denser than water and has no business floating -- yet laid flat on still water it sits in a shallow dimple, until one drop of dish soap touches the surface and it drops instantly to the bottom. The answer is that the skin-like tension of the surface was holding it, and it was never buoyancy. T2: why a liquid has a skin at all -- a molecule down in the bulk is pulled equally from every side, while a molecule at the top has neighbours only below and beside it, so the surface is dragged inward and behaves like a stretched sheet. T3: what soap does -- soap molecules crowd into the surface and wedge between the water molecules, cutting water's surface tension roughly in half; that is why soap makes water WET things it would otherwise bead off, and why a drop of soap in a plate of peppered water blasts the pepper to the rim. T4: Agnes Pockels, barred from university in Germany because she was a woman, built her instrument at the kitchen sink: a tin trough of water about seventy centimetres long, a sliding strip to sweep the surface clean, and a small button hung from a balance to measure the pull. In 1891 she wrote to Lord Rayleigh in England describing what she had found, and he had her work translated and published in Nature. T5: what her trough actually measured -- a film of oil poured on water spreads until it is a single molecule thick and then stops; the area at which the surface tension suddenly changes tells you how much room one molecule takes up, and Pockels put it near twenty square angstroms. A kitchen sink measured the size of a molecule. Further rungs: a falling raindrop and a soap bubble are round because a sphere is the smallest possible skin around a given volume; capillary action, where water climbs a narrow tube against gravity because it sticks to the glass harder than to itself, higher the narrower the tube, testable with a paper-towel corner in a saucer; mercury doing the opposite, beading up with roughly six times water's surface tension and curving the wrong way in a tube; and the surfactant lining the lungs' alveoli, without which the smallest air sacs would collapse -- the physics that keeps premature babies alive.
source: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' (accessed 2026-08-11) -- water about 0.0728 N/m at 20 C against mercury's 0.465 N/m; the unbalanced-inward-pull molecular account; capillary rise h = 2*gamma*cos(theta)/(rho*g*r) and the contact angle, with mercury's convex meniscus and depression; spheres minimising area for a given volume; alveolar surfactant countering collapse; Young and Laplace as the nineteenth-century theorists. Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels' (1862-1935) -- barred from university education on grounds of sex; the roughly 70 cm rectangular metal trough with a sliding strip and a button on a balance; the 'Pockels point', the minimum area a molecule occupies in a monomolecular film, put near 20 square angstroms; the 1891 letter to Lord Rayleigh and the resulting Nature paper 'Surface Tension'; the trough as direct ancestor of the Langmuir-Blodgett apparatus; the 1932 honorary doctorate from Braunschweig.
framing_note: The sub-strand's KID-REPLICABLE flagship: nearly every rung is an invitation, and the paperclip rung should read as a dare rather than a fact. Accuracy rail: a floating paperclip is NOT buoyancy, and the ladder must say so in plain words -- steel is far denser than water, the unbroken surface is what holds it, and the soap destroys the surface rather than the steel. Second rail: describe the instrument Pockels actually built; she was a rigorous self-taught experimenter with a purpose-made apparatus, not an amateur who got lucky, and 'a woman in a kitchen' must never be the joke of the rung. Dinner-test payoff: T1, which a kid can run in two minutes with a glass of water. Distractor mine: buoyancy and Archimedes offered as the wrong reason for the paperclip -- the most seductive wrong answer available; 'soap makes the water heavier'; 'the paperclip is hollow'; plus genuinely adjacent real physics (adhesion versus cohesion, capillarity, the Marangoni effect) as near-miss options. Teach 'surface tension' and 'molecule' before testing them.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank already answers 'a thin film of water pulling by surface tension' in a T2 rung about a red-eyed tree frog gripping a wet leaf -- so no creature may be the SUBJECT of any rung here, and water striders and pond skaters are animal's, not science's. COOKING owns kitchen chemistry -- the soap-and-pepper and oil-film rungs must be framed as physics demonstrations, never as cooking technique.

name: You never suck a drink up a straw
scope: The mechanism that puts the whole sub-strand in the kid's own hand at every meal. T1: drinking through a straw involves no pulling at all -- you thin the air inside your mouth, and the atmosphere pressing down on the surface of the drink pushes the liquid up the tube. The answer is that the outside air pushes it. T2: the ten-second test that proves it -- poke a pin-hole in the side of the straw above the liquid line and you can suck as hard as you like and get nothing, because the air now has an easier way in. T3: there is a hard ceiling on the whole business. Even a perfect vacuum in your mouth could raise water only about 10.3 metres at sea level -- roughly a three-storey house -- because that is the tallest column of water the atmosphere's push can balance. A twelve-metre straw is impossible for anyone, of any lung strength, forever. T4: the discovery. The Grand Duke of Tuscany's well-diggers in Florence found their suction pumps simply refused to lift water past about ten metres, however well made. Galileo wrote about the problem in Two New Sciences in 1638 and got it wrong: he thought the column of water broke of its own weight, as though water had a measurable breaking strength. His student Torricelli saw what was really happening -- the pump had never been pulling; the air had always been pushing, and ten metres is all the air can lift. Further rungs: a siphon, and why water runs uphill out of a fish tank and keeps going once started; why a straw would fail in a spacecraft cabin at zero pressure, and why astronauts drink from squeezed bags; why every deep well has its pump at the BOTTOM, pushing, rather than at the top, pulling; and a vacuum cleaner, which pulls nothing at all -- the room's air rushes in through the nozzle and carries the dirt with it.
source: Wikipedia, 'Suction' -- 'when a straw is used to suck a liquid from a glass into the mouth, the atmospheric pressure on the fluid in the glass pushes the liquid up through the straw along the pressure gradient'; the theoretical sea-level maximum of about 10.3 metres / 34 feet for water. Wikipedia, 'Suction pump' -- the practical limit of about 10 metres (32-34 feet); the Duke of Tuscany's Florence fountain and well problem; Galileo in Two New Sciences (1638) proposing that 'the column of a water pump will break of its own weight when the water has been lifted to 34 feet', and the article's statement that this explanation was incorrect; Torricelli's 1643 resolution attributing the limit to atmospheric pressure rather than vacuum resistance. Wikipedia, 'Barometer' -- mercury about 14 times denser than water, hence a 76-80 cm column instead of about 10.5 metres.
framing_note: MECHANISM ladder, and the one that makes the entire sub-strand personal. THE accuracy rail: never write that suction 'pulls'. The whole ladder turns on the word PUSH, and a stem that slips into pulling language destroys the rung. Second rail, and the ladder's moral centre: GALILEO -- the hero of most of the physics strand -- got this one wrong, and his own student fixed it; say so plainly rather than softening it, because that is the bank's skepticism-of-your-own-heroes commitment in action. Dinner-test payoff: T1, with T2 (the pin-hole) as the dare that settles it in ten seconds. Distractor mine is unusually good here: 'suction is a pulling force'; horror vacui; 'your tongue works as a pump'; capillary action and surface tension, both real physics and both wrong for this; and best of all Galileo's own answer, that water has a breaking strength -- a wrong explanation held by a genius, which is exactly the sort of distractor this bank wants. Lane inside the strand: the mercury barometer, the Torricellian vacuum and the weather belong to the TORRICELLI ladder; this ladder owns the straw, the pump, the siphon and the 10.3-metre ceiling.

name: Auguste Piccard: the same physics highest and deepest
scope: One man, one equation, run in both directions -- the sub-strand's natural capstone. T2: on 27 May 1931 Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer rose from Augsburg to 15,781 metres and became the first human beings to enter the stratosphere. What made it survivable was not the balloon but the passenger compartment: a sealed, pressurised aluminium sphere, the first ever built, and the direct ancestor of every airliner cabin. T3: the inversion. Piccard saw that the same idea turned upside down would work at the bottom of the sea, and his bathyscaphe hung a crew sphere beneath a large tank filled not with air, which would have been crushed, but with GASOLINE -- lighter than water, and unlike a gas, barely compressible at all. To sink you released gasoline; to rise you dropped iron shot. T4: on 23 January 1960 his son Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh rode the Trieste down to the floor of the Challenger Deep, about 10,900 metres, where the water presses more than a thousand times harder than it does at a beach; on the way down a window cracked with a bang and they carried on. T5: why gasoline and not air, spelled out -- a gas halves in volume when you double the pressure, which is Boyle's law again, so any air-filled float would have collapsed and stopped floating long before the bottom, while a liquid barely changes volume and keeps its buoyancy all the way down. A stratospheric balloon and a deep submersible are the same machine run in opposite directions: a light fluid trapped in a bag, and ballast you throw away. Further rungs: the 1932 flight to 16,201 metres; the 1953 dive to 3,150 metres with Jacques; and Herge modelling Professor Cuthbert Calculus on Piccard's appearance in the streets of Brussels.
source: Wikipedia, 'Auguste Piccard' -- the 27 May 1931 ascent from Augsburg with Paul Kipfer to 15,781 m, the first humans to enter the stratosphere, in the first pressurised aluminium gondola, carrying cosmic-radiation instruments; the 1932 flight to 16,201 m; the bathyscaphe FNRS-2 using gasoline as flotation rather than fuel because liquids remain effectively incompressible under extreme pressure, with releasable iron ballast for resurfacing; the 1953 dive with Jacques Piccard to 3,150 m; Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh taking the Trieste to about 10,911 m in the Challenger Deep on 23 January 1960; Herge's Professor Cuthbert Calculus drawn from Piccard's appearance during his Brussels years. Corroborated on the gas-compressibility reasoning by Wikipedia, 'Boyle's law'.
framing_note: A CONCEPT ladder wearing a biography: it forces buoyancy, gas compressibility and pressure-with-depth into one story, which is why it earns the T5 ceiling. THE accuracy rail: the flotation fluid was GASOLINE used as a float, never as fuel -- the sources are explicit and the rung must be too, because a kid will otherwise assume an engine. Dinner-test payoff: T3, a submarine that floats on petrol. Distractor mine: 'air tanks', helium, styrofoam, and 'a pump that empties the hull' -- the last being a real method used by ordinary submarines and therefore the best wrong answer available; plus Beebe and Barton's tethered bathysphere, a real adjacent vessel that had no buoyancy engine at all and simply hung on a cable. VERIFY-OR-DROP at build time: the Trieste crew's reported sighting of a flatfish at the bottom is disputed by biologists and is animal-adjacent -- prefer to leave it out entirely; and any rung on Bertrand Piccard's 1999 non-stop balloon circumnavigation must be checked against a primary source before use. Lane: GEOGRAPHY owns the Challenger Deep as a PLACE, so key every rung to the vehicle and the physics.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank owns the Challenger Deep and the Mariana Trench as a place, including a T5 whose answer is 'It is deeper than Everest is tall' and which handles the subduction geology -- never make the trench's depth, location or geology the answer here; key the bathyscaphe, the gasoline float and the ballast. ANIMAL owns deep-sea creatures and the nautilus buoyancy story, including a rung already answered 'a submarine' -- no creature rungs, and no 'what human machine works like this animal' framing.
